'Cause, like, you're basically- - That's exactly it. - ... there's no, like passive low energy thinking. - No. - You're like- - There's no coasting. - ... problem. - There's no coasting. - Solve problem, next problem, solve problem, and you're really thinking. - It's funny. It's actually very similar with racing. There's some tracks, like Le Mans, where you get time to relax. There's the Mulsanne straights where it's kinda long. You're going fast, but in a straight line, you can take a breath. And then there are other tracks where it's just coming full on all the time, and you don't have any moment to relax, and you stumble out of the car after an hour in each, and it's very different how exhausted you are. And this is exactly what I'm finding with the agents too, that when you're running at max human capacity- ... you're just constantly in a corner. - Do you think people are in danger of burnout? - I think the moment we're in right now is gonna pass. That this need to... It's not a babysitting motion, but constant interaction with the agents is gonna fade. From what I've seen on Omarchy, I think we can automate a ton of the development and debugging of the system- ... to the point where I can just review that email once a day, and then make the decisions once a day. Yep, goes, no, goes, in, out, and whatever. We're not there yet, but I think we're gonna get there. - Well, can you sort of, like, empathize with the feeling that, say, a young person sitting in San Francisco, everybody around them is not sleeping. They're obsessed. They're programming nonstop. And there's this kinda sense, that AGI is gonna be here any minute. There's, everybody knows somebody who's made millions of dollars because they sold a startup. And so there's a kinda feeling like you shouldn't be sleeping. You should be constantly managing agents and programming and building and, and that feels like a moment in time we'll look back at. - It's the birth of a new paradigm. It's always messy. - It's always messy. - It's always exhausting. There's no other way around that. And by the way, hasn't San Francisco always been like this? I remember the dotcom boom years, and everyone was just the same, and then it was all mobile, and before that it was the gold rush. So I think that's probably- ... just San Francisco. It attracts- ... the kind of individuals- - The dreamers - ... who would, who would think, "I don't have time to sleep." I've not been on that track, generally speaking, but I will admit that the last three months have felt more exhausting than any other project I've done in the last five years, since the Hey launch. That was the last time we had a crazy exhausting launch. - Do you think you can keep going at this pace? - No, no, no, no, no. This is not sustainable at all. - Okay. - But I also, I can see the end of the tunnel. Because the automation, which by the way, everyone is building. This is so hilarious. Like, everyone is building their little gas town, their little agent coordination, their setup. This is all gonna be solved. We're not all gonna have to build our own coordination harnesses. Of course we're not. And in fact, I'm a little surprised that it's gone this long, that there's not more of it has been sucked up by the major labs. You'd think that they'd just built this stuff in. But some of it is also this is what a new domain looks like. I remember for a hot moment when JavaScript kind of came to realize its own power, and there was basically a new JavaScript framework every five minutes, right? Like, a lot of churn. This is what happens at the advent of a new paradigm. So I think it's natural, and I think it's gonna settle down, and I can already see the light at the end of the tunnel. So I don't mind a sprint. In fact, I welcome it now. I like this notion that most time is calm, but then occasionally you gotta climb a mountain. - If we look back to the DHH a year ago, what advice would you give to that guy? - I wouldn't wanna spoil it. - Okay. - What a- ... thriller that this has been. I mean, if you would've scripted this, I'd be like, "This is so far-fetched. Get out of here. Unbelievable," right? I wouldn't wanna know anything. The fact that this rollercoaster and this acceleration has been absorbed in real time by everyone, no one knew, right? Like, some had premonitions that were a little better than others, but no one knew, not exactly the way- ... it was gonna go and how fast it was gonna take off. I mean, it's the show of a lifetime. I mean, the mean cinema- ... absolutely applies- - Yeah, it's incredible. - ... to this moment. - Uh, that said, what do you think DHH from a year from now will be like? I mean, what are the possible versions? - That all our dreams are coming true. Like, this is the AI maximalist abundance argument. That once Elon's robots have the level of intelligence and AGI that I'm experiencing on some of this development stuff, the world is gonna be so unrecognizably different that we can't even imagine it. Now, I don't spend any time thinking about that because I think that is the way to the AI psychosis. So therefore, I just immerse myself in the moment and get absolutely the maximum out of it and- - Just have fun. - Just have fun. I mean, I get it why people are finding this exhausting. Just keeping up. Not even using agents, just, like, being like, "What's the latest model? What did, what tool are we using now? Is it TMox? Is it a Herder? Is it none of it? Is it agents?" Whatever. I get it, but I also again think we should be so blessed. You are alive in this moment where decades are happening- ... in weeks. - Um, quick bathroom break. I've been generating a lot of video recently with Higgsfield, and so they, they became a sponsor. Created a racing video. Wanted to get your opinion on it. - Oh, yeah? Oh, let me see. Let me see. - To see, um- - If they downshift on a straight like they do in the movies, I'll call it out. That is the worst. Let me see. - Yeah, see if- - Oh, that's a real clip - ... this is fully AI generated. So first it goes- - Wait, what? This is AI? - Yep. - Shit, that's my suit. That's my car. - Lights go green on a street that never sleeps. - Oh, my God. - Do an audio- - Are you kidding me? - But they never came. Is it good? I got a bad case. - I mean, it's crazy. You really have to notice in the... Like, that car didn't have headlights on and the other one did. And that looked like a 60-year-old version of me. But holy crap, the... Wow, that was crazy. - So there's parallels here to programming because if you do just straight video generation with no human in the loop- ... you get a lot of weird artifacts- ... and so on, and you can't really do... So they do and I highly recommend people go to the Higgsfield YouTube. They have full 90-minute original movies. And, like, I can't look away. It's really cool. 'Cause it used to be that it's just, like, something that just feels like trailers. Like advertisements for something. - Yes, yes. - This is actually telling stories, like, people's faces and they're talking and you're like, you're drawn in. It's not quite where programming is. And so the question is how do you integrate the human into the loop of the filmmaking process? So you have to create the people, and they're- ... they have to be kept consistent. And then for the images that are kinda like feeding the thing in the creation process, you have to correct through prompting things that don't feel right. Because when you go from image to video, the stuff that doesn't feel right will be- - It's gonna be zoomed up, right? - That's the stuff that's- ... going to really create, uh- ... the non-realistic stuff. The questions I had for you is, like, do you think outside of programming, can you apply lessons from programming to video creation, to art? - It's a good question because I think good art is very dependent on the same thing that good software is depending on: having a vision, having a cohesive idea of what you wanna create. How is it different? How is it novel? How is it going to appeal to people? But I'm not sure that the creative instincts transfer quite as well. Um, I don't know that I would have the creative insights to come up with good video prompts that would create compelling content. But it's funny because I have actually, on TikTok, there's this guy, I'm trying to remember, Goblin something. That creates these... They are shorts, but not super short, maybe a couple minutes, of really interesting sci-fi vignettes. And I think the guy is actually working on a feature-length video right now. Um, and I think that this is one of those abundance moments. There are creative people with that vision all over the place, especially in a genre like film, where before it required a $200 million budget to create, I don't know, a sci-fi movie. Now suddenly, with AI, if you have the right vision for it, you can do that in your bedroom. Now, that story's been told quite a few times in other domains. It used to be true that if you wanted to record a studio album, well, you needed a studio, and you needed to book that. And now you can record at home on your laptop, and you can do a lot of these things, right? So we've had this democratization process happen with plenty of other domains, but film seems to be one of the last ones. - And it's the one that makes, like, me and a lot of people feel weird, right? Like- - Oh, I'm super excited 'cause I think it's- - I mean, you- - There's so much garbage being produced right now. It's the same argument with the slob, right? So people for a second were worried about slob in programming, and I was telling them, like, "Have you seen the human slob? It's also pretty bad." And I think if it comes to studio entertainment, I mean, the bar is pretty low, right? Like, the number of great movies I've been dying to see over the past, say, five years, not been a particularly high number. - Yeah, the video models are just, they're able to create incredibly realistic facial expressions. I mean, it just might change the nature of film I think they're— I guess my hope would be that video games and film kind of merge, and that film can become interactive - Like the malleable operating system, having the malleable narrative, having malleable entertainment, that man, Game of Thrones, what if we could just forget the last four episodes of slob that was produced- ... and then AI- ... comes up with- ... I don't know- ... maybe 100 different variations, and someone else watches that, and I get the version that actually finishes off that show in a way that's fitting. - Yeah. Something tells me an individual creator would not create those la- would create a different ending for Game of Thrones. - Oh, for sure. Right? And more just to make the argument that talk about human slob. That was an absolute atrocious ending to perhaps one of the greatest pieces of, Movie history, I was about to say, but, um, series history, right? It was so good, and it was actually a compelling argument for the fact that you need that strong vision. And as soon as those showrunners had to go without a script, it went off the rails. - Do you think... You've mentioned AGI. Do you think we've actually achieved AGI? - No, not in the general definition that it's in all the things. But have I seen AGI in these glimmers? Absolutely. Especially over the last three months, I've seen things where I was thinking to myself, like, "How would AGI look different from this?" - Right. - What, what more could there be? And I mean, I can quibble at the margins, but on the big picture, I've seen it able to do these long run tasks and coordinate these multiple aspects of it that we're so far beyond that early moment where I'm telling it, "Go do this, package that." And now it can carry out a whole task from these vague instructions. That feels very AGI-like, and that's what's so inspiring about the moment because you catch these glimmers. And then you go, "What if everything was like that?" - Doesn't programming basically unlock the everything? So you can write a pro- like it can generate the program that does the everything. - So, so this is... I'm in that meta phase right now. So I'm building this Amabot system that's managing the development of Omarchy, and I'm using AI to build the bot. And I'm seeing that recurrent loop where I started it on, like, "This is what I want. I want you to be able to have these isolated VM workers and so forth," and then it can do the self iteration. Then it starts running it. It starts noticing its failures. It starts optimizing it. And a lot of that system, Amabot in particular, AI has driven the majority of the design decisions. Like, I had some vague ideas of where I wanted. I wanted to use this brains and hands pattern where the model is running from where the code is executing- ... which is actually a really interesting pattern. Again, Toby alerted me to that, where you have a coordinator that runs the model- ... but it's manipulating a safe VM where any untrusted code you're pulling down from pull requests or issues or whatever can't contaminate the model. And even in that loop, I keep seeing it catch itself, spotting vulnerabilities, where it's like, "Oh, I actually just took some feedback from a test run. If a clever attacker had embedded a malicious payload in the response of the test run, that could have polluted something. I took it for good thing. I better start treating that as as outside data." And you just go like, it is just... I get why San Francisco is so obsessed with fast takeoff- ... because clearly they've seen this 100 times- ... more. They've seen it with all the models that are in- ... training now, and we keep getting these little glimpses, like the security breach with Hugging Face, where OpenAI was training this model, and the model starts inventing ways, essentially sending smoke signals to itself through embedding messages in a package manager, where you just go like, first, that's damn clever. Second, okay, that's also a little scary. And third how amazing would this be if we could harness this level of intelligence- ... and ingenuity towards productive ends? So this is the it's so over, we're so back pendulum that keeps swinging back and forth- ... that AI has just delivered that swing back and forth like nothing else. Like barely a week goes by where it has to swing one way, and then the next week it swings back the other way. Exhilarating. - I'm still at the stage where it makes me truly happy to see those moments of cleverness, and they're becoming more and more frequent. Just kinda like seeing, oh, like first of all, at the very basic level, when a model gets it. - Yes. - I'll say a basic prompt, you know, a request, and it, it doesn't just do a dumb implementation. It deeply understands, and it... That was... That's a, that's always a beautiful thing. It's almost like having a good, like, partner, like program. - That's exactly what it is. That's exactly why it's so exhilarating and why, as we talked about before we started, it can sometimes be difficult to come out of hyperdrive. That's also one of Toby's terms here. That when you're working directly just one-on-one with agents and you're not looping in other humans, you go so fast, and when the agents are really understanding your intent, or even better, they revise and improve upon your intent to deliver something that was greater than what you asked for And you're doing this with 16 parallel threads. It can be quite difficult to come out of hyperdrive and have to deal with squishy humans. They just, they don't think as fast. They don't move as fast. And I mean, I'm trying mostly to make light of it, but you can also see a dark version of that where someone does end up in an AI psychosis where they're not interested in other humans at all anymore. I mean, certainly don't have that at all, but I do have this sensation at times where I'm really grateful for just the rush of just me and the agents. Like, can I just not talk to anyone else but agents- ... for four hours? Like, that's an incredible run. - Toby is such a fascinating human because he's running a large company. So I would love to get insights of how AI's being incorporated effectively in companies. Because, like, for me, humans are pretty slow. And so, and so there's a temptation to, like, use AI for basically, You know, AI running inside Slack, for example, or inside, The Basecamp, whatever. And, like, collecting all the information about the human interaction, basically handholding the humans to speed up as much as possible. And like, and then at a certain point you're like, wait, what is this human... What are each of us doing that's not replaceable by AI? And that becomes, like, a scary kind of conversation because a lot of work is kind of replaceable. - The irony here is it already was. So the number of fake email jobs that currently exist in this world is an absolute epidemic. And- ... this, by the way, is not a new thesis. Um, David Graeber wrote this wonderful piece Bullshit Jobs, back in, I think it was maybe early 2010s. Based on a poll he did in the UK asking people, at that time, would... I think the question was something like, "Would it make a difference if you didn't go to work?" For humanity, for mankind. And something like 30-some percent answered, "No, it wouldn't." That a third of workers thought that their job was fake, that it did not produce any worthwhile, valuable outcomes, neither for the community or society or maybe even the economy at all. And this was my argument since day one with startups. This was why we stayed a small company. This was why we didn't want to take VC, because I was so skeptical of the idea that you could get hundreds of programmers, thousands of programmers to do something productive- ... as a collective group. And I think what we're seeing right now with some of the layoffs is a testament to that, not AI. It's just that during the pandemic, a bunch of overhiring went on, and now AI is a convenient excuse to slim down. But I do also think AI is going to expose some roles as just not being productive ways for humans to spend their time, and therefore we must come up with new ways of spending their time. And the one, again, I'm quoting Toby for the third time here, but anecdote that he shared me, or observation was, okay, let's say we all-- we lose half the jobs that are currently happening right now. Do you know that Formula 1 employs literally tens of thousands of people just to run cars around in a circle for spectators? Like, that has, that whole circus has no intrinsic value to society besides the spectacle it produces of amusement and entertainment. We just decided it would be really fun for these, what is it, 12 manufacturers to create these fast cars and constantly tweak their little aero improvements, and we will watch it, and we will spend literally billions of dollars doing it and employ tens of thousands of people towards an ultimately deeply frivolous activity. So if we are liberated from a bunch of drudgery and fake email jobs, maybe we all get employed as F1 style engineers and drivers and mechanics and masseuses and the other 1,500 jobs that are involved in that, and we come up with new things. I think this is... Humans are very poor at imagining what exactly the future's gonna be like. - Yeah. Imagine, imagine a future 100 plus years from now, where we look back at this whole span of history, thousands of years where humans worked. - Funny thing is we're already doing that, right? Like, the number of fake email job people who sit on a chair all day long and type into a machine who don't have hard physical labor would be unimaginable- ... to folks in the 1800s, right? So the future is always already here, it's just not evenly distributed. - Unfortunately, as is always the case, the transformation of society required to go from one step to the other is going to have a lot of suffering. And potentially political turmoil and all that kind of stuff. Because you can imagine how many white collar jobs might be lost in this process. - Yes. And I don't think you should make light of that. I don't think it's funny. But I also do think it's a necessary component of progress. And I think if we look back upon the Luddites or the folks working the fields, separation has a tendency to reduce empathy. So we have high empathy right now because we know people- ... and we are people who are facing these challenges. But- What is our empathy for the Luddites of the early 19th century? Would we wish that all garments were still made by hand weaving? No, we wouldn't. We want the comfort and accessibility and convenience of being able to buy clothing off the rack. So we must suffer in the moment for future generations to live more prosperously. And that's always been true - ... I think that's actually the trick, is to push for progress but have deep compassion for the people who have to suffer. And that's many of us. The suffer the transformation required to achieve that progress. And sometimes too often in places like Silicon Valley or so on, you can over-focus on, look, the kind of utilitarian view of things- ... and look at the progress. - Right. - But, you know, considering deeply each individual human that suffers because of that progress is important. - I do think that suffering becomes more meaningful when you are suffering for a future someone in particular, like your kids. And I think this is one of the great tragedies of the moment, is the falling birth rates are making it more difficult for people to be excited about a more prosperous future that is difficult to get to. Because if we're planting trees of which our children will not sit in the shades, I don't know, maybe we should just make some lumber and burn it all down, right? I think there's a nihilism that can sneak into society much more easily when we are not DNA invested in the future, when we are not liable to our own offspring to propel forward. So I think these are bad trends to merge at the same time, that we have these falling birth rates and these problems with coupling, and the fact that we need to keep our chin up about the future and be... I mean, you don't even have to be excited about it in this literal ecstatic sense that I'm portraying here, but I think you should be hopeful, and I think you should be working towards that hope, and I think it's much easier to do so when you have literal skin in the game. - We've been talking about AI agents. Let's talk about the human side. What what do you love most about being a dad? - That's a good question. I think the overall love that expands from humans that derive directly- ... from your lineage- ... is very difficult to communicate because I was actually not a particularly big kids person prior to the arrival of my own. And now they are the most interesting people in the world. A lot of the time. Not always. Sometimes they're also just assholes and so forth. But there's been such a focus on, "Oh, kids are the worst. Look at all the things I can't do. I can't go out and drink. I can't do this. I can't do that." Yeah, that's called sacrifice, and sacrifice is meaningful when you're doing it for something worthwhile. And what could be more worthwhile than literally the continuation of the human species? And that you having a stake in that. Now, there's also just the sheer joys of watching a human grow from a baby to a toddler to a teenager. My oldest has just become a teenager. And I often talk to Jamie, my wife, about this, where the regret I would have of having missed that opportunity on the last day would just be total, unlike anything else. So I do think it is far more satisfying even in the moment that is normally portrayed. Again, as I say, there's such a focus on all the ways they suck. "Oh, you don't get to sleep," or whatever. "They're annoying. They're ungrateful." Yeah, yeah, these things are all true, but the sense of meaning you get from it is unparalleled. And I'm excited about a lot of things. I love building things, and I love hobbies, and I love all sorts of stuff. But creating life with another human that you love is literally the peak experience of being on the planet. - What do you think about them coming up in this world full of AI? Is it totally diff- It feels like, maybe I just sound like an old man on a porch, but it feels like a very different world. Y- So I grew up before the internet, but even the internet doesn't feel like as big of a transformation as this. - No. But there's been bigger transformations. I mean, imagine growing or being born in like 1880. Imagine seeing the First World War and the Second World War. Imagine seeing the airplane, the radio- ... television. I mean, the transformation, and I think Peter Thiel makes this argument, that basically nothing has happened in the physical world in quite a long time. We've been stagnant. All the development has been in the digital realm. And as important as that is, it's actually not as consequential as we like to believe it is. Maybe AI will be that thing that is more consequential. It does seem to point that way. But there are other humans at other times who have lived through- ... transitions that for them certainly would feel as momentous as what we're living through. And I think having that sense of history, that you're not that special in your sense of worries, in your anxieties. This was one of the great revelations of discovering the stoic writings. You have these guys 2,500 years ago dealing with very familiar dilemmas and challenges in their life, and recognizing that we're not so special in that regard, I think is a great liberation. Because then you think, "Okay, well, we have whatever, 200,000 years of human development before us, and they somehow made it through." - Yeah. And, um- - We will make it through. - ... the thing that makes life worthwhile is basically the same today as it was- - Yes. Yes. - ... 2,000 years ago. - Yes. Love, creation, creativity. - Yeah. Same challenges. - I read this book The Fourth Turning. You check that out. It talks about this notion of history working in cycles, and there are these, phases to history, and they name them and so forth. And the specific theory is not as important as just realizing that this is a... History is a circle, more so than just a straight line. And we are repeating many of the same patterns over and over again. They feel so unique to the moment. And whatever crisis we're dealing with right now feels so pressing and important until we zoom back a little bit in history and realize that the last one also felt so pressing and important to the people who lived through it. - Yeah. You're making me feel better. So I'm gonna travel across the country and spend a lot of time with no access to the internet, alone with my thoughts. - I think that's healthy, taking a break. - It's okay. It's okay. - I took not a big break, a little break, break from Max this summer, three weeks. - Yeah, you were... You disappeared off of- - I'm surprised you noticed. - I went through withdrawals. No. Uh, you disappeared for, I don't know, a few weeks. - About three weeks. - Three weeks? What happened? - Um- - This is after, after Llama. - I've done that before. I just sometimes get

items.title: Khabib Nurmagomedov: Dagestan, MMA, UFC, Islam, Conor, Fedor & Football | Lex Fridman Podcast #500
items.transcript_text: - The following is a conversation with Khabib Nurmagomedov, one of the greatest fighters of all time, who retired from the UFC undefeated with a perfect twenty-nine and O record. It was a huge honor for me to meet him, to train together, and to have this deep conversation. We had this conversation entirely in Russian. This was my first time doing so on this podcast. And even these words I'm saying right now are spoken in Russian. So if you're hearing me in English, you're actually listening to the English dub. On YouTube, you can switch between language audio tracks by clicking the settings gear icon, then clicking audio track, and then selecting the language you prefer. For the original Russian version, select Russian. And for the English dub, select English. Subtitles are also available in both languages. The translation and dubbing are a collaborative effort of translators, real human beings, including myself and AI. Thanks to the incredible team at ElevenLabs for their help. And now, please allow me to take this moment to say thank you from the bottom of my heart for your love and support all these years. I love you all. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. And now, dear friends, here's Khabib Nurmagomedov. Let's try in Russian if we can, like you suggested. - I can help you out if you need. - Yeah, thanks, brother. I kind of feel it in my heart and soul, but sometimes I can't find the right words. - I know, brother. We got this. - Great. Let's start from the beginning. So that gym back in Dagestan where you trained is legendary for its spartan conditions. There was just one shower for seventy people, only cold water. And yet, this humble little gym managed to raise more than twenty world champions, including several UFC champions. Can you try to explain or maybe reflect on what factors in that gym, those training sessions, that life in Dagestan created so many champions? - Sure. So we're talking about the gym, the one located in Makhachkala. And Makhachkala, for the people who don't know, it's the capital of Dagestan. This was back around the years from two thousand to two thousand and ten, and even later on. In twenty nineteen, we opened up a big gym, a major facility that is still functioning to this day. But before twenty nineteen, we all actually trained in that gym where there was practically nothing. It was just a school gym with nothing but mats, a single punching bag, one climbing rope, and a kind of indoor basketball court. And if we go even further back, before two thousand, before we moved to Makhachkala, we lived in a village. In the village, we had a gym right inside our house. My father, he built a gym at home, and he was training all the local village kids right there. And there were times back when I was a child, let's say when I was maybe six or seven years old, I would occasionally wake up to the sound of, people training, doing their drills right there in the gym. You know, like with judo or freestyle when they're drilling, one guy throwing another. Those are my first conscious memories. I was maybe five, six, seven years old at that time. So my father set up this gym in the village and trained local kids, including me, my older brother, and all our close and distant relatives, anyone who wanted to come. A lot of kids came to him. - So you would wake up and there are these sounds. - Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You hear the hitting, the throwing over and over. And my father's voice, how he's shouting, giving instructions, pushing someone, coaching, teaching. I lived with those sounds. But that was in the village. And later when we moved to Makhachkala, well, you couldn't say the gym there was wow either. There were only mats. And of course, the most valuable thing an athlete can have, a coach, my father. So he trained us there. And to be honest, let's say, until I became a champion and had big success, we never had a good big gym where we could, you know, all take a shower together at the same time after training. We always had just one shower for everyone, no proper amenities. - So your life story began in the mountains of Dagestan in Sildi, then Kirovaul, and then Makhachkala. And in all these situations, there are very interesting stories. But one of the things I heard you say is that the best results are born out of the worst conditions. What can you say about that? Philosophically, is it correct to say that comfort is kind of the enemy for champions? - It depends on the sport. For example, let's say in football, you have to have conditions. You can't really play if there is practically no field. Of course, you can play in the dirt, and it happens sometimes. You can start there. But when you are ten or twelve years old, you already have to be at a certain level. You must have conditions. But if we look at our sport, then what is the most important thing? The coach. You also need sparring partners who will push you in the gym, as they say, right? And you need the mats. Our sport is not expensive. You just buy your wrestling shoes, singlets, shorts, a T-shirt. And if there's a mat, you wrestle, you become a champion, you fight. But when you live too well, let's say, you know, you're never in need. For example, you were born into a wealthy family and you already have everything. Would that same wealthy father, would he force you to do such a brutal sport? You always want to watch Ronaldo play. You always want to watch Beckham play. You want to watch Edgar Davids running around the field in those glasses, his hair bouncing behind him, right? You still wanted to watch the way Barthez played in goal. No matter how many bizarre goals he conceded, you still wanted to watch him play. Or Oliver Kahn, the way he stood in goal and directed the whole team, the way he would rush out to the ball, the way strikers were afraid of him. I mean, so many strikers have admitted that they were afraid if they found themselves one-on-one with Oliver Kahn in the penalty area. You always wanted to watch Roberto Carlos take a free kick or storm down the left flank. You always wanted to see Cafu or Michel Salgado make an overlapping run. The way Vieira stood there as the defensive midfielder or somebody like Maldini or like Rio Ferdinand or somebody like that, you wanted to watch Casillas in goal. So, you know, for me, and maybe for our generation, those players had something special. - Can you try to explain what charisma is? Like you said, there are good players, and then there is Zidane. - It's very difficult to explain. You either have it or you don't. Personality, right? - Yes, but there are so many different forms of it. Zidane, in a way, almost moved slowly, in a way. - But he'd carry the ball from midfield into attack incredibly quickly. So it's very hard to put into words, hard to explain it. - And both Ronaldos had that. I mean, the Brazilian Ronaldo too, the way he played in those World Cups. It was just phenomenal. - '98, 2002. Even in 2006 when he was already past his peak. He was so fascinating to watch. Seriously, how many people turned on their TVs just to watch Ronaldo? People knew that was it, that in 2010 he wouldn't be playing. And even in 2006, he wasn't really in his prime. But still, so many people turned on the TV just to watch him play. And Zidane, 2006 was really, you know, the peak of that whole generation of legends that had been building since '98, 2000, 2002, and '04. All the cream of the crop came in. Most of them weren't at their physical peak anymore, but the names were still there. Honestly, I think that for football fans, I'd recommend just looking up the teams and the lineups from the 2006 World Cup. Look at the rosters. Every single team had stars you wanted to watch. - Speaking of teams, what style of football do you like? You prefer short passing, long balls, individual plays, you know, like Maradona carrying the ball or, of course, Cristiano Ronaldo taking the ball and scoring himself? - Mostly those who take the initiative. - You like that? - Yeah, definitely. I like players who are willing to take the initiative. I was recently talking to Zlatan about this, and he said, "It drives me crazy when I have players on my team who, when you pass them the ball, they immediately get rid of it. They don't want to take the initiative." When you have three or more players on the team, if there are three people on the team who are not afraid to make mistakes, that's usually enough. They take the initiative, take control of the game, drive the team forward, make mistakes, but they keep trying. And then there are others who hide, he says. They get the ball and immediately pass it to someone else. Just don't give it to me. Not me. Not me. They just want to get rid of the ball. It's like... You know, it's like something one of Zidane's coaches once said. If you don't know what to do with the ball, give it to Zidane. He'll figure it out, so... You see, that's the thing. It's a quality not every player has. You're taking the ball. You're taking responsibility. You're taking the initiative. You are not afraid to fail. You're not afraid to make a mistake. Cristiano had a moment like that. He missed a penalty, and later in the same match, he stepped up to take another one. Think about that. You take the first penalty. You miss it. Then another penalty comes along, and you still step up to take it. Because if you miss two penalties in the same game, you're under a lot of pressure, right? But that's the point. You're not afraid to fail. As a leader, you take the initiative, and you're you're willing to take risks. That's honestly the beauty of it, the beauty of sports in general. The bigger the risk, the bigger the potential for greatness. If there's no risk, then there's no... You can't make, can't put yourself in the category of athletes people will talk about as some of the best ever. - Especially when it's a high-level game like the World Cup and... - Yes. The more risk, the sweeter the victory. There must be risk. - That's why they often speak of Maradona as a great player. There are many great players. He's great- - One of them, yeah - ...for many reasons. But one reason is that he kinda, kinda carried the team on his shoulders. - He took the initiative and carried them. That's, that's when he led Napoli, you know? When he led Napoli to the league title. Who knew Napoli then? Maradona came from Barcelona to Napoli and made them champions, and the whole stadium was named after him. Many guys played in Napoli, but there was never anyone like Maradona. And recently, I saw somewhere, or I think someone pointed out, the pressure on the guys who are transferring to Napoli. Whoever you are, you will always be in Maradona's shadow, and you stay in the shadow because fans will never give you the credit you might deserve because they will always compare you to him. Are you Maradona or not? And if you're not Maradona, you will never get full recognition. - I want to say that one of the things that makes Messi great, I think, is that he really had to live in such a shadow of Maradona, and especially with the World Cup. - Yes. - It's not easy. - And he came out of it. - Hard to emerge from that shadow. - Yes. And he won the World Cup, yeah. In that sense, you have to give Messi his due. I'm addressing the Real Madrid fans now. Ours, yours, both sides. - You're explaining it to them. - Yeah, yeah. - I got you. - Most of them, I think even if they don't like Barcelona, they still recognize Messi's greatness. - I know that you met Zlatan. You talked to him. I think he's one of the most, most self-confident people in football, in the world in general. What do you think about this confidence? Of course, he's joking around a little bit, but I think he really believes in himself. - Well, yeah, he does. He does. I've known Zlatan for years now. We get along well, and I know his kids, and I like his personality. I like his confidence. I mean, he's a unique player. There are not many Zlatans in football. You know, wherever he played, he always scored. He's a goal scorer. He is that kind of center forward, and he always carried the team. He was a leader wherever he transferred. It doesn't matter. Milan, Inter, Juventus, when he moved to LA Galaxy or Paris Saint-Germain. He was a leader everywhere he went, with the national team, with his clubs. He was always the guy driving the team forward, taking the initiative. And honestly, he cemented his place as one of the greatest players to ever play the game. And yeah, maybe he was... When it comes to trophies, not individual achievements, but team honors, Sweden wasn't such a Wasn't exactly the greatest team, and some of the clubs he played for didn't always win the biggest trophies. But as an athlete, as an individual, as a person, he is a very strong athlete. - We talked a lot about Dagestan, talked a lot about America. You're in Dubai a lot these days. Do you like it there? Also, you have spoken very highly about Sheikh Hamdan. What do you like about Dubai? What do you like about this region? And what do you respect about Sheikh Hamdan? - Our team's been in Dubai for seven to eight years now. We train at the Nad Al Sheba Sports Complex. The NAS Sports Complex, this is under Sheikh Hamdan's office. It's like his home, his place. We train there, we eat there, we live there. Sheikh Hamdan helps us with everything and takes care of us. The way he treats us, what he does for us, his support is just limitless. He supports us in everything, and it's not just one, two, or three years. It's already been seven or eight years. And I am very, very grateful to him. The way he welcomed us, took us in, and helped us, continues to help, it's hard to put it into words how grateful we are. Our entire team is very grateful to him, and he knows it. So in general, Dubai has become... Actually, the Emirates, Dubai, and Abu Dhabi have become like a second home for us. And so it happened that over the last six or seven years, the UFC has been holding events in Abu Dhabi, and the PFL has been putting on events in Dubai. These are two of the biggest MMA organizations in the world, and a lot of our guys compete there. We arrive before the fight, we stay, we do training camps, they compete. We are incredibly fortunate that we have support at the government level. In Abu Dhabi, we've been supported by Sheikh Mohammed, Sheikh Tahnoon, and Sheikh Mansour. And in Dubai, Sheikh Hamdan has really taken us in like his own team, like younger brothers. In that respect, we've been incredibly fortunate, and our entire team is deeply grateful for their support. - And they've created a country that has become one of the world's central hubs. People from everywhere travel there. - It's unique, right? The local population is only around one and a half million people, actually even less than that. But, you know, there's such an influx of tourists, people, business people, major events, and everything happening in terms of business and sports is just incredible. What's happening in Dubai and Abu Dhabi is, it's like nothing else. The only places you could really compare it to are major global cities like New York, London, Paris, Tokyo. But those are huge metropolitan areas with populations of well over twenty million people, and they have centuries of history behind them. And here, they've built cities, an entire country really, in just a few decades and turned it into a kind of magnet. It's like a magnet that attracts everyone. The country's location, its logistics, the sheer number of people coming in, not just visiting, but wanting to move there, live there, and start businesses, it's remarkable. It's a unique place in today's world. With everything that's happening around the globe right now, this country really stands out because of the opportunities it offers. It's unique in that sense. - Now I'd like to ask you this. For you, your Muslim faith and God, it's obviously central to your life and to who you are. Can you explain what role God plays in your life? - Well, first of all, I was born, raised, and brought up in a Muslim family, in a Muslim community. Since childhood, religion's always been the most important thing for me. And when I say religion, the first thing I mean is Salah, Namaz. And my entire life in general, my daily routine, the way I lived, trained, studied, and everything else has always been built around Salah. The rest was scheduled around it. Even today, when I was choosing time for this podcast, I knew we'd be talking for a couple of hours, so I deliberately picked a time right after the midday prayer. I pray, come here, finish up here with you, and then go pray again. That's how my life's been, and still is, and that's how it will continue to be, I hope. I've always tried to organize my life around worship, because first and foremost, my purpose in this life is to worship the one God. Everything that happens after that is, it's secondary, so to speak. And faith in God and learning more and just striving to get closer to God, that continues throughout our entire lives. So in that regard, I'm very grateful to the Almighty for opening this door of understanding and reflection for me, for helping me realize that we are all servants of God and that our purpose in life is to serve one God. - And as you were explaining that helped you in your career in the sense that, you know, psychologically, by keeping you from letting success go to your head? - That helped me with everything. I've always placed my only hope in the Almighty. Whatever situation I might face, I've always believed that only the Almighty can truly make it easier for me. And when it comes to not letting success go to your head, not becoming proud, not becoming full of yourself, religion and my faith in Allah have helped me with that too. I truly believe that only faith can help a person get through life's hardest trials. And sometimes I think about people who suffer the loss of a loved one, someone very close to them. For example, when I lost my father, I remember thinking to myself, "If I didn't believe in the Almighty, if I didn't have faith in God and understand that it was predestined, that we all come into this world and then leave it, that no one stays here forever, that no one belongs to anyone, and we all belong to the Almighty, and that we will all return to Him, I don't know how I would have coped with it." I'm a very emotional person. I think it would have been extremely difficult for me to go through all of that without faith. In that sense, I feel fortunate to have this understanding. - So faith really helped you when you lost your father? - This was the only thing that helped. Nothing else worked. I know a couple of people who have lost someone very close to them, and they struggle to accept it. They would ask, "Why? Why? Why?" So many questions. I told them, to answer that question, you need to go deeper into religion and try to understand why were you even born in the first place, and why do these thoughts even come into your head? And what if you didn't have any thoughts at all? What if you couldn't think, couldn't understand anything? These thoughts, this awareness, your mind, your abilities, none of that was there before. Then it appeared. Why? That's the question. None of us existed. Then we were born. We were little. We weren't aware of anything. We didn't remember anything. Then little by little, we grew up and became adults. We became successful, became somebody. We became who we are. So why did all of this come specifically to you? There are so many questions like that. And so these questions are, let's say, a kind of guide through life. And for me that's what religion is. It guides me and helps me. - You often say, "Alhamdulillah, all praise to God." That's very powerful, that sense of gratitude. Can you tell us, can you explain why you say it so often? - You know the saying, the tongue speaks what the heart is full of. The way you speak shows what's in your heart. If you have something dark in your heart, your words will show it, no doubt. We all have some dark parts in our hearts. Every single person has them. Sometimes they come out in what we say, how we express ourselves, what we share with people, and so on. Everyone has that. But if your heart is mostly good and pure, then that will also be reflected in your speech. And And I just like praising the Almighty and giving all the credit for my success back to Him because everything we have is given to us by the Almighty. Throughout the history, there have been many people who made big mistakes after becoming successful, powerful, and wealthy, and they started saying, "No, no, this happened to me because I'm so great, because I'm so, I'm so intelligent, because I had vision, because I've got the brains, because I'm extremely capable. That's why all of this came my way." But at the same time, there were many others who worked just as hard, who weren't any less intelligent, and the Almighty just didn't give it to them. He chose you and gave it to you, and you just have to give the credit back to Him. You shouldn't take the credit for yourself. That's what I believe. And it's something I've come to through studying my religion. I understand that everything the Almighty has given to me is not because of who I am. It's simply something God has given me as a test to test me and, in the end, see which of my deeds outweigh the others, the good or the bad. Because as a believer, I believe that there will be judgment and everything we have, everything we do, every action we take, we will be held accountable for it. There will be a day of judgment, there will be scales, and everything will be weighed. - What advice would you give young people about life and their careers? Millions of people are watching you and deeply respect you. What would you say about how to live your life? And how do you find your path and stay on it? - Well, I wouldn't want to speak just from my own perspective. I'd rather bring people back to the scripture, to what the Almighty said, "Read." That's the first word revealed in the Holy Quran. The first command is read or ikra. So to everyone listening to or watching this podcast, I would want to bring them back to that. Read, meaning what? Educate yourself, observe, learn, improve, but don't stay in one place. And anything a person is truly looking for, if they genuinely want to find it, not just find an answer, but find the truth, they can reach it, but they can never reach it without reading. They need to read. When a person reads, what they read enters them into their body, their heart, their mind, and it triggers a search. A search for knowledge begins inside them, but if you don't read, you won't find anything. Just listening to someone is one thing, but reading is something different. So my advice would be read and find within yourself the strength to come closer to one God and seek to understand why we were sent here in the first place. Today, you and me, we're almost the same age. So let's just think about this. For example, my grandfather on my mother's side passed away in two thousand and three. Now it's twenty twenty-six. He's been lying in the grave for twenty-three years. And then there was his grandfather, or let's say his great-grandfather who also died and has been in the grave for over a hundred years, roughly speaking. But what about people who died two thousand years ago? They've been in the grave for two thousand years. What's next? It's a good question, isn't it? They've just been in the grave all this time, and that's it. So what was the purpose of their life? A person has been in the grave for two thousand years, but maybe lived for seventy years. Roughly speaking, let's say one hundred. They lived for one hundred years and have been in the grave for two thousand. So what matters more, those one hundred years or these two thousand years? And what happens after those two thousand years end? People believe different things, whether there is a day of judgment or not. That's where the difference lies between a believer and a non-believer. After everyone is resurrected, there will be the day of judgment. There will be judgment, and after that, people will enter eternity. Eternity compared to eternity, what are two thousand years? They're nothing. And we live for, let's say, seventy years. And many people choose those seventy years over eternal life. And if a person understands that these seventy years they have here, roughly speaking, seventy or eighty years are meant to be used to prepare for what comes after, so that when the day of judgment arrives, and after that judgment they can live forever, not in hell, but in heaven. If that becomes their ultimate goal, then they will strive to do good deeds because they will fear the day of judgment. And that's really what life is about, preparing yourself for the day of judgment. - That's true. To truly understand life and its deeper meaning, you have to think about eternity. Only then can you really understand your role. - Actually, it can keep a person away from evil. From evil and, and it can stop them from treating other people badly. It can hold a person back. But if you don't have that understanding, if a person lives completely convinced that there's nothing after death, what's there to stop him from doing evil? Just like that. What do you think? And on top of that, an even more dangerous combination. You become powerful, wealthy, and you become famous. What now? Suddenly every door is open to you. Just imagine a person like that. And on top of all that, he doesn't believe in the day of judgment. He doesn't believe he'll be held accountable for his actions. That's, you know, it's like a nuclear bomb. He can end up causing harm to people everywhere. But if you know that for everything you have here, you'll eventually have to answer, that there will be a day of judgment and that you'll be called to account, and if you fail that test, you'll burn in hell forever. That'll make you rein yourself in a little. You'll have to take that into consideration. You'll have to tighten things up a little. You'll begin to understand that you're not nearly as important as the image you've created of yourself in your own mind. You start becoming more, as Americans say, down to earth. You become more grounded. You're not flying, you're walking on the ground. - You once put it beautifully. You can allow money and fame to stay in your hand, but not in your heart. You've still got many years ahead of you, but you're already an example of someone who's become famous, made money, and remained the same person. - If money stays in your hands and not in your heart That's a good thing. But the moment it gets into a person's heart, it corrupts them. Once it's there, it's very difficult to pull it out of your heart. If you have wealth in your hands and use it properly for good causes, for the right purposes, for people in need, for your family, relatives, friends, people from your hometown, that's a good thing. But as soon as that wealth gets into your heart, it becomes very difficult to share it with others. And this is a very dangerous place for a person to end up. And I'm sorry, but as a believer, I believe that most people in hell will be wealthy. - One of the reasons millions of people find you so interesting to watch is that you're constantly growing. First, you were a great fighter. Now you're becoming a leader. Your wisdom just keeps increasing. You're evolving as a person, but still the core values remain. It's good to see, inspiring for people. Money and fame haven't changed you. You're just growing as a human being, as you always have. - I hope it's in the right direction. It's just, the thing is people only see the good. They don't see the bad. And we all have the good side and the bad side. Everyone, sadly. And especially when it comes to celebrities, we only show the best side of ourselves. Even when you post photos, you only post the good ones, the pictures where you look your best. So I hope that the way people see me, as you pointed out, is the way I really am, because it's difficult to judge yourself objectively. You're always biased when it comes to yourself. That's how it is. We tend to think highly of ourselves, right? You can't really see yourself objectively. We hide our flaws and put our best qualities on display. Sometimes people even start believing in a fake version of themselves. For me, I try to stay on the honest path throughout my life to remain true to who I really am and to show my true self to people. Maybe not everyone agrees with my behavior, my opinions, my worldview, or my attitudes toward, towards sports, religion, and other things. Not everyone shares my views. Not everyone is a fan of mine. There are people who, let's say, see me very differently. So I'm just... I've tried, I continue to try to be who I am. That's all. And I hope that my ending will be a good one, too. Well, you know, at least that's my hope. - You've stayed the same, but you've also grown. I mean, today you even managed to say something nice about Barça. So see, that's progress. Yeah. Well done. - Come on, without Barcelona, there wouldn't be Real Madrid. If the Spanish league didn't have either Real Madrid or Barcelona, it just wouldn't be the same. They've been competing against each other for how many years? One hundred twenty. It's hard to imagine Barcelona and Real Madrid without each other, and so is the Spanish league without that rivalry. It's impossible to imagine. So yeah, we have to give you some credit, but Real Madrid is the royal club. Come on. It's the best. You know? - And thanks to both of them, we've been able to enjoy truly incredible football for so many years. - For so many years, yeah. - Um, Khabib, brother, I don't even have the words to explain how honored I am that you're here talking with me today and showing me so much warmth. There's no way to fully express what you mean to millions of your fans around the world, including me. Thank you so much for everything. Thank you for this conversation. - Thank you. Thank you very much, Lex. - Thank you for listening to this conversation with Khabib Nurmagomedov. And again, thank you for everything. I love you all. Goodbye, my friends. See you next time.

items.title: Gary Gallagher: American Civil War, Slavery, Lincoln, Grant & Lee | Lex Fridman Podcast #499
items.transcript_text:
- You cannot control what a great military event can set loose. More battle casualties than US forces had suffered in every war combined down to that point happened in two days. Two and a half months after that, George B. McClellan's army engaged with Lee's army in what came to be called the Seven Days Battles at Richmond, 36,000 casualties. So those two together just showed that this was gonna be on a totally different scale. He added a psychological twist. What, what Grant envisioned his doing, and Sheridan actually did it in the Shenandoah Valley before Sherman did it in Georgia, is go into an agriculturally productive area, burn the mills, kill the livestock, destroy the crops, lay waste to it so that it can't be a logistical support of the Confederacy anymore. Sheridan did it in the Shenandoah Valley, and then Sherman did it in Georgia. But Sherman said, "But I'm also going to break them psychologically. I'm gonna show them that my army can go wherever it wants to go whenever it wants to go, and there's nothing Jefferson Davis can do about it." The great forces are all that matters and individuals don't really matter notion of history I think is ridiculous. Individuals really matter. For the United States, Lincoln and Grant matter beyond calculation- ... in this war. And on the Confederate side, if you take Lee out of the picture, the war doesn't last nearly as long as it does. In terms of causation, if you take slavery out of the picture, there is no Civil War, period. - The following is a conversation with Gary Gallagher, a historian of the American Civil War. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. To support it, please check out our sponsors in the description where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. And now, dear friends, here's Gary Gallagher. The American Civil War broke out in 1861. What were the causes of the Civil War? Could it have been avoided, or was it inevitable? - I don't know if anything is inevitable in history, but it's certainly safe to say that the conditions were in place to make it possible- ... by the winter of 1860, '61, and the conditions that made it possible were all related to the institution of slavery and its effects both in the states where slavery was allowed and the states where it was not allowed. And there had been a series of tensions that grew in the decade preceding the 1850s. It's not that one side wants to get rid of slavery and the other side wants to protect slavery. I'm talking about the white people in the United States now who would be making the political decisions. It's a question of whether slavery was going to be able to expand into federal territories. That is what really created the starkest difference between the two sections in the 1850s, even in the late 1840s. The issues that came to most, uh, perilous a point in the view of many people then had to do with whether slavery would be allowed only where it already existed, or would it be allowed to expand. If it could expand, then it seemed that it might be conceivable at some point even that the slaveholding states could end up with a majority. They were in a minority by 1860, '61 and feeling beleaguered, feeling threatened. They'd long since lost the population race to the free states. Early in the nation, the most powerful states were slaveholding states. Virginia was by far the most important state. Four of the first five presidents were from Virginia, all slaveholders, all prominent members of the slaveholding class. Those days were long gone by the late 1850s. - So that's an important thing to say. It wasn't before the Civil War a discussion about abolishing slavery. It's about whether slavery, the institution of slavery should be expanded. - Allowed to expand into federal territories. There, there is a portion of the white population that is adamantly in favor of getting rid of slavery immediately. The abolitionists, they... There was even a political party called the Liberty Party, that ran a candidate in 1840 and they got a handful of thousand votes. They reached their high point in 1844. They got about two and a half percent of the vote. The abolitionists are a tiny minority among the— even in the North, tiny minority among the white people of the United States. The African American population, nearly four million of them by 1860, of course, would have embraced it instantly and yearned for it. But in the white population, the abolitionists are a tiny minority. They are much despised even across much of the North because they were seen as agitators who roiled the Union and deepened rifts that might bring a significant political break. - So how did this escalate to a civil war, this almost policy discussion about the institution of slavery? How did it actually escalate? - It escalated into a civil war because in the presidential election of 1860... There'd been two party systems in the United States. The first party system, the Republicans, the Jeffersonian Republicans versus the Federalists. After that, there was, the two parties were the Whig Party against the Democratic Party. The Democratic Party grew out of the Jeffersonian Republican Party. It's the same party. The Whig Party foundered to a significant degree on the issue of slavery. How do you maintain a national party that has a wing in the Southern states and has a wing in the Northern free states that can handle the issue of slavery? The Democrats managed to do that. The Whigs could not do it, and so the Whig Party ran their last candidate in 1852, presidential candidate, significant candidate. And the Republican Party emerged in the mid-1850s, took most of the old Whigs into the Republican ranks and one of the Republican, the key Republican platform plank was no expansion of slavery into the territories. Not abolish slavery, no expansion. That was the key in 1856 when they ran their first candidate. In 1860, that is again the key plank in the Republican platform. The Republican platform in 1860 says where slavery exists it will continue, but it cannot expand into the territories. When white Southerners saw that, that meant that they were doomed to become an increasingly minority section in the nation, and you would have a federal government increasingly dominated by the free states that could then do the one thing that the white South could not countenance, and that is tamper with the institution of slavery in the South. The presidential election of 1860 brought the destruction of the last national party, which was the Democrats. They couldn't even settle on a candidate, so you end up with a Northern Democratic candidate running, Stephen A. Douglas, and a Southern candidate running. The convention fractured and John C. Breckinridge ran on the, on the Southern Democrat platform. You had a Unionist candidate running who just didn't wanna talk about slavery, let's talk about the Union, and you had Lincoln running as a Republican. When Lincoln won, the white South looked at Lincoln winning. Here's a guy who has said that he doesn't think slavery would expand, but he'd said more than that. He scared the white South more because in 1858, both Lincoln and William Henry Seward, these are two prominent, prominent Republicans, had said basically in separate speeches, the House Divided Speech on Lincoln's part, the Irrepressible Conflict Speech on Seward's part, that the nation could not continue in the long term half slave and half free. And everybody in the South knew which way they wanted it to be. They would want it to be no slavery. And so Lincoln's election scared the white South enough so that seven of the 15 slave-holding states seceded in response to Lincoln's election. They seceded between December 20th, when South Carolina went out, and the end of February. You had the deep South went out. - What was the general view amongst the populace towards slavery? Let's kind of lay it out. Let's you know, for the audience looking back, let's put ourselves in the mind space of how people saw the world, how people saw slavery, how people saw African Americans. - Well, the baseline among the white Americans, there were about 31, shade more than 31 million Americans in 1860 for the census of 1860. About four million of them were African Americans, three and a half million of those enslaved in the South. Anyway, among the white population, the average attitude toward Black people is what we would call profoundly prejudiced. Doesn't matter whether you... And that just changed everything. - That was the real turning point. - That was a huge military turning point, and then on the heels of that, Philip Sheridan won a series of crushing victories in the Shenandoah Valley, the last of which came just before the election, and it was Sherman, and to a lesser degree Sheridan, that reelected Lincoln, and not just Lincoln, but huge Republican majorities- ... in both the House and the Senate in 1864. - And then the thing that broke the back of Confederacies, Sherman's March, 60,000 men across Georgia to the sea, burning the infrastructure. - Yes, as he said, "I'm gonna go across and make Georgia howl," is how he put it. He added a psychological twist. What Grant envisioned his doing, and Sheridan actually did it in the Shenandoah Valley before Sherman did it in Georgia, is go into an agriculturally productive area, burn the mills, kill the livestock, destroy the crops, lay waste to it so that it can't be a logistical support of the Confederacy anymore. Sheridan did it in the Shenandoah Valley, and then Sherman did it in Georgia. But Sherman said, "But I'm also going to break them psychologically." That's what he said, that, "I'm gonna show them that my army can go wherever it wants to go, whenever it wants to go, and there's nothing Jefferson Davis can do about it." He said, "When they decide that, they'll give up." Didn't exactly work that way, but that's what he-- so he marched first to Savannah, and then the final campaign for Sherman was up through the Carolinas. He went up through South Carolina and into North Carolina. And Grant laid siege to Lee, and the siege lasted nine months, the Siege of Petersburg in Richmond, and finally Grant broke Lee's lines on April 1st, 1865. Lee started a retreat. Grant just gave him no pause, and he ran him to ground at Appomattox after about a week, and Lee surrendered. - What do we know about the relationship between the two men?
